```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      message = FALSE, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.3)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
root <- ".."
table_dir <- file.path(root, "outputs", "tables")
fig_dir <- file.path(root, "outputs", "figures")
read_result <- function(name) {
    file <- file.path(table_dir, name)
    if (!file.exists(file)) stop("Missing output: ", file,
                                 ". Run the R scripts first.")
    data.table::fread(file)
}
show_table <- function(data, digits = 3, caption = NULL) {
    knitr::kable(data, digits = digits, caption = caption,
                 format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
}
```

# Executive summary

National health surveys provide important evidence about mental distress, but
national prediction accuracy can mask differences in performance for smaller
population groups. This study evaluates whether three classifiers trained on
pooled national BRFSS data perform comparably for **AI/AN-alone adults** and
**other identified single-race adults**, and whether performance differs before
and after 2020.

The analysis uses a previously assembled BRFSS 2014–2024 analytical file
with 4,790,742 records and 25 selected variables. The main outcome is
frequent mental distress (FMD): reporting 14 or more mentally unhealthy
days in the previous 30 days. Associations and performance differences are
descriptive; this study does not establish causal mechanisms or clinical harms.

# 1. Research questions

**Primary research question:** How well do models trained on pooled U.S.
BRFSS data classify frequent mental distress among AI/AN-alone adults
compared with other identified single-race adults, and does performance
differ between 2014–2019 and 2020–2024?

**Supporting questions:** How did the prevalence of FMD differ between
periods across the two populations? How did physical-health, demographic,
and socioeconomic characteristics relate to FMD, and did selected
associations vary by group or period?

# 2. Background

BRFSS is an annual, repeated cross-sectional health survey of U.S. adults.
FMD captures frequent self-reported poor mental health, not a clinical
diagnosis. CDC analyses of earlier BRFSS surveys documented mental-distress
differences across racial and ethnic populations and lower distress among
respondents with greater socioeconomic resources (CDC, 2004). An analysis
of the 2018 BRFSS showed substantial FMD differences by disability status
(Cree et al., 2020). These findings motivate studying physical health and
socioeconomic characteristics, not assuming they cause distress.

Health surveillance research has emphasized that aggregate AI/AN samples
may be small and cannot reflect every Tribal community (Adakai et al., 2018).
Healthcare algorithm research has also illustrated how overall model behavior
can mask group-level problems when proxies or evaluation targets are
poorly aligned with health needs (Obermeyer et al., 2019). That healthcare
algorithm studied a different outcome and population; it motivates careful
subgroup evaluation rather than establishing an AI/AN bias in the BRFSS models.

**Population definition:** The analysis classifies respondents reporting
AI/AN alone separately from respondents classified in other identified
single-race categories. Multiracial and unknown-race categories are excluded
from this primary two-group comparison. The comparison group should not be
interpreted as necessarily free of Indigenous ancestry. The available
calculated race-alone indicator cannot identify all AI/AN respondents who
also report another race.

# 3. Data, outcome and methods

The original pooled dataset was previously created from 11 annual BRFSS files.
The reproducible RStudio pipeline starts from that archived file; it does
not re-extract the XPT sources.

The binary outcome uses MENTHLTH responses: 14–30 days = 1; 0–13
days = 0. BRFSS code 88 ("none") is zero days, while codes 77 and 99
("don't know"/refused) are missing.

Predictors are physically unhealthy days, general health, income,
education, age, recorded sex and the study period. They are measured
contemporaneously, so classification here is not prospective clinical
prediction.

The project uses a common train/test split stratified by year, group and
outcome, with three shared cross-validation folds, followed by a held-out
evaluation in both periods. Model training and evaluation use
sampling-adjusted weights to account for computational caps on the much
larger comparison group.

The primary prevalence estimates use the historical notebook's pooled
weight formula. Alternative pooling approaches are reported as
sensitivity checks. This is not an endorsement of a unique official CDC
multi-year weighting formula. The reported model metrics are weighted
descriptive estimates; no complex-survey confidence intervals are
automatically claimed.

# 4. Descriptive exploration

## 4.1 Retention and availability

```{r retention}
show_table(read_result("02_group_retention.csv"), 0,
           "Group-by-period sample retention.")
```

**How to read:** Compare `n`, `outcome_valid`, and `complete_predictors`
within each group; complete-case exclusion may not affect every population
equally.

## 4.2 FMD prevalence

```{r prevalence}
show_table(read_result("02_prevalence_by_group_period.csv"), 2,
           "FMD prevalence (%) by population and period under three weighting choices.")
```

**How to read:** Each percentage describes respondents reporting 14+
mentally unhealthy days. Values are estimates from repeated cross-sectional
surveys, not within-person changes.

```{r annual-plot, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "02_annual_fmd_trend.png"))
```

**How to read the graph:** Each point represents one year. The dashed
vertical line indicates the start of 2020. Higher values indicate a larger
estimated share of respondents reporting FMD. The lines do not establish
causes for changes.

# 5. Unsupervised learning: PCA

PCA was fit using dummy-coded predictors in a training subsample, excluding
FMD as an input. The first two components summarize axes of variation in
the recorded predictor combinations.

```{r pca-variance}
show_table(head(read_result("04_pca_explained_variance.csv"), 5), 2,
           "Variance captured by leading principal components.")
```

```{r pca-plot, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "04_pca_scores.png"))
```

**How to read the graph:** Each point is one respondent. Points close
together have similar encoded predictor values. Overlap is expected and
does not itself mean that health outcomes are the same. The displayed PCA
sample is a computational subsample, not a nationally representative map.

```{r pca-loadings}
loadings <- read_result("04_pca_loadings.csv")
loadings[, magnitude := abs(PC1)]
show_table(head(loadings[order(-magnitude),
                         .(variable, PC1, PC2)], 8), 3,
           "Predictor encodings with the largest absolute PC1 loadings.")
```

Large absolute loadings indicate which encoded predictors most strongly
contribute to the first PCA dimension; the sign of a component is arbitrary.

# 6. Supervised learning

## 6.1 Three-model comparison and cross-validation

The models were: ordinary logistic regression, LASSO-penalized logistic
regression and random forest. All three were evaluated using the same
cross-validation folds. Hyperparameters were chosen by mean CV AUROC.

```{r cv-table}
selected <- read_result("06_selected_configurations.csv")
show_table(selected, 4,
           "Cross-validation winners (higher AUROC is better).")
winner <- selected[which.max(cv_mean_auroc)]
cat(sprintf(
    "The highest mean cross-validated AUROC in this run was achieved by **%s** (%.3f).",
    winner$family, winner$cv_mean_auroc
))
```
Cross-validation scores select models; independent held-out scores are
the primary evidence for performance across population and period.

## 6.2 Held-out performance by group and period

```{r performance}
m <- read_result("09_heldout_model_performance.csv")
show_table(m[, .(family, study_period, cohort, n, events,
                 auroc, average_precision, brier,
                 sensitivity, specificity, calibration_gap)], 3,
           "Held-out model metrics by group and period.")
```

**Metric guide:** AUROC and average precision summarize ranking quality
(higher is generally better). Brier score measures probability accuracy
(lower is better). Sensitivity is the fraction of actual FMD cases
classified positive; specificity is the fraction of noncases classified
negative. The reported classification threshold is 0.20.

```{r auroc-plot, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "09_auroc_comparison.png"))
```

**How to read:** Compare the group points within each period. The distance
between the points is a descriptive difference in discrimination. It does
not by itself establish algorithmic discrimination or the source of the
difference.

## 6.3 Does the group gap change across periods?

```{r gap-change}
show_table(read_result("09_change_in_auc_gap.csv"), 4,
           "Change in AI/AN-minus-comparison AUROC gap (post minus pre).")
```

A negative result means the AUROC difference became more unfavorable to
AI/AN-alone respondents in the later period. These are **observed
differences**, not automatically statistically significant changes.

```{r gap-interpretation, results="asis"}
gap <- read_result("09_change_in_auc_gap.csv")
if (all(gap$change_in_auc_gap < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    cat("All three fitted classifiers showed a more negative AI/AN-minus-comparison AUROC gap in the later period in this run.")
} else {
    cat("The magnitude and direction of changes varied across model families in this run.")
}
```

## 6.4 Calibration

```{r calibration, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "09_calibration.png"))
```

**How to read:** The dashed diagonal is ideal agreement between predicted
and observed FMD. Points above the line mean the model predicted a lower
probability than the actual observed rate for that bin; points below the
line mean predicted risk was too high.

# 7. Associated factors and limitations

```{r association, results="asis"}
file <- file.path(table_dir, "05_adjusted_predicted_probabilities.csv")
if (file.exists(file)) {
    show_table(read_result(basename(file)), 2,
               "Exploratory covariate-standardized FMD predictions (%).")
} else {
    cat("The exploratory association results were not run.")
}
```

The regression-based associations are exploratory and contemporaneous.

```{r feature-signals}
signals <- read_result("09_predictor_signals.csv")
signals[, magnitude := abs(value)]
top_signals <- signals[order(family, -magnitude),
                       head(.SD, 6), by = family,
                       .SDcols = c("term", "value", "type")]
show_table(top_signals, 3,
           "Largest-magnitude signals within each model family.")
```

Positive logistic coefficients indicate higher fitted log odds relative
to their reference values, conditional on the other model terms. LASSO
coefficients are penalized; forest impurity importance has an entirely
different scale and may favor variables with more possible splits.
Coefficient magnitudes therefore should **not** be compared directly
across model families.

Key limitations include the use of AI/AN-alone race categories rather
than all AI/AN combinations, changes in survey coverage and measurement
over time, nominal income brackets across years, incomplete source-level
certainty about all year-specific harmonizations, and lack of
design-based uncertainty intervals for model-performance gaps. The
historical source-file audit identified four differences between an
independently calculated 2024 FMD category and the saved outcome; that
issue should be resolved or disclosed before any claim of perfect
source-category agreement.

# 8. Conclusions

The core evaluation tests whether models trained on pooled national data
show comparable held-out discrimination and probability accuracy for
AI/AN-alone respondents and the other identified single-race comparison
population in two time periods. Findings should be summarized directly
from the generated performance and gap tables, with the limitations
above. Model-performance differences alone do not establish their
causes or demonstrate real-world clinical harm.
